1:
A new discourse begins here, and two voices explain why. Gill has the prophet, having finished his parables and closed with a gracious promise, entering on a fresh discourse of reproof: what had been delivered in parables having had no effect, they are now called to hear the Lord in more clear and express terms. Calvin explains the abruptness by the way the prophetic books were made: the prophets did not literally write what they delivered, but what we have are collected summaries of what they were wont to address to the people, whose slowness was such that the same things had to be repeated daily. He then voices the complaint he expects: we heard yesterday a discourse on the mercy of God, and now he fulminates against us, so he must be changeable. His answer is that men must often be awakened, because forgetfulness creeps over them and nothing is harder than to lead them to God; they cannot be taught except he reproves their sins, and then, lest they despond, gives them hope of mercy, and then returns to reproofs, which is the mode of address in all the prophets. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same turn structurally: what the first part exposed symbolically is here detailed both in its nature, the apostasy prevailing through the ten tribes, and in its consequences, the destruction of the kingdom and rejection of the people, while within this chapter the reproof passes from Israel as a whole to the sins of the priests.

The controversy is taken by all as a legal one. Clarke calls it a lawsuit in which God is plaintiff and the people defendants, and answers his own question about when God has a controversy with any land: when there is no truth, nor mercy, nor knowledge of God in it. Ellicott makes the position sharper, a judicial suit in which Jehovah is plaintiff as well as judge, the children of Israel being the northern kingdom as distinguished from Judah. Henry opens the scene as a court set, and asks whom God may expect to give him a fair hearing but his own professing people; they are ready enough to hear when he speaks comfortably, but are they willing when he has something to lay to their charge. Sin, he says, is the great mischief-maker, and some actions lie against his own people which do not lie against other sinners: breaking covenant, bringing a reproach upon him, and returning ingratitude for his favours. He notes the order too: the controversy is pleaded by the judgments of his mouth before the judgments of his hand, so that he may be justified and may make it appear that he desires not the death of sinners. Calvin draws the practical conclusion, that men in vain flatter themselves when they have God against them, the dispute being announced so that they may reconcile themselves while a seasonable opportunity is given.

What the land lacks is counted in three terms. Ellicott would render the second as love rather than mercy, since the Hebrew word covers both the love of God for Israel under the covenant and the answering quality in a man. Henry treats the first two as justice and charity, the weighty matters of the law: the generality seemed to have no sense of the thing called honesty, making no conscience of what they said and did though it were injurious to their neighbour, much less any sense of mercy or of an obligation to pity and help the poor. He makes the third the root of the other two, since it is not strange that there is no truth and mercy where there is no knowledge of God; and he finds the aggravation in the privilege, that this was the land in which God had made himself known. Clarke adds only that all three refer to the minds of the people.
2:
The list of crimes is read against the commandments. Keil and Delitzsch note that the enumeration begins with infinitives absolute, setting forth the acts with greater emphasis, and match the items to five of the commandments; the perfects which follow, they add, are not preterites but express a completed act reaching from the past into the present. Gill and Calvin both stop at the first word. Gill reports that some join the first two terms into the single sin of false swearing, but holds that swearing itself is meant, taking in cursing, profane oaths and the divine name taken in vain, and chiefly perjury, which, though a kind of lying, is distinguished from it here. Calvin knows the same two readings, forswearing or deceiving by swearing, and prefers a third: since the word often means to curse, he does not doubt that the practice of cursing, then common, is what is condemned.

Why the sins are itemised is Calvin’s question. The wicked do not easily bend their neck: they first murmur, then clamour against wholesome instruction, and at last rage with open fury; so the prophet shows by particulars in how many ways they provoked God, as though anyone comparing their life with the law would find them avowedly fighting against him. Then comes the point that gives the charge its edge: these are not such thieves and murderers as are led in our day to the gallows, but men in high esteem and eminent in wealth, the only illustrious men among the people, and it is these the prophet brands with the disgraceful names. Clarke traces the crimes to the three things wanting in the previous verse: where there is no truth there will be lies and perjury; where there is no mercy, killing and murder will be frequent; and where there is no knowledge of God, private offences prevail until stealing becomes public robbery. On the last clause he has murders not merely frequent but mutual, men going out to kill one another, and, no law being regarded, the kinsman slaying the murderer. Ellicott, who notes that the charge suggests the Decalogue, puts it as murder added to murder with ghastly prevalence, and Wesley as slaughters so multiplied that the end of one is the beginning of another.

That the judgment falls on the animals is felt as a difficulty. Calvin raises it directly: some object that it is unworthy of God to be angry with miserable creatures which deserve no such treatment. His answer is that since beasts and birds and fishes were created for the use of men, it is no wonder God extends the tokens of his curse to all creatures above and below when his purpose is to punish men. Keil and Delitzsch put the relation the other way: the words affirm not merely that creation suffers by the sins of men, but that the depravity of men causes the destruction of the other creatures, since God gave man dominion over the beasts and the earth to be used for his glory, and punishes wickedness by pestilence or devastation. They and Gill trace the mechanism to drought, the mourning of the earth following want of rain, or else, as Gill allows, grass and corn trodden down by a foreign army. Wesley supposes the cattle starved for want of fodder consumed by the armies, and the fish taken away by the drying up of the waters. Ellicott calls the whole a judgment of famine, with plague on fish as well as murrain on cattle and starvation among the birds. Clarke explains the loss of the fish differently, that the shoals which at certain seasons frequent the coasts and are caught in millions may be turned by the unseen influence of God to avoid them, as he says has often happened, so that a source of supply and wealth is shut up.
4:
Who silences whom is the first difficulty. Gill would render the clause as the words of the people themselves, forbidding the prophet or any other to contend with them or reprove them for their sins. Calvin hears the complaint of the prophet, who deplores a people that would bear no admonitions, like men past hope who admit no physicians; it is a proof of irreclaimable wickedness, he says, when men harden their hearts against all salutary counsels, and things were such that none dared reprove the public vices. Ellicott takes the words as prediction rather than prohibition, the voices of wise counsel being silenced and Ephraim left alone in his obstinate wrong-doing. Wesley says they are so hardened it is to no purpose to warn them any more, and that they will contend with their teachers and reprovers. Keil and Delitzsch explain the opening particle from a tacit antithesis, that with so much depravity there would be much to punish, but punishing would be useless; and they reject the construction which takes the second term as an object, since it yields no meaning in harmony with the rest.

That second half is where the voices divide most sharply. Ellicott reports the rendering given by nearly all versions and commentators, that the people are as those who contend with a priest, as guilty as men who defy his injunctions; but he prefers a repointing which suits the denunciations of the priest in the verses following: thy people, O priest, are as my adversaries. He admits the objections and holds them not insuperable. Clarke notes that one of his oldest manuscripts omits the word for priest altogether, in which case the text reads simply that thy people are as rebels, the word being added in the margin by a later hand. People and priest are alike rebels, he holds, the priests having become idolaters as well. Calvin knows a reading that takes the particle as affirming rather than comparing, so that they altogether strive with the priest, and prefers the comparison: the prophet calls the people the censors of their own pastors. Froward men become insolent when reproved, and ask whether they are to be treated like children; we daily meet with many such, who boast of their knowledge as though superior to all prophets and teachers.

The fall that follows ends the argument. Calvin takes the connective as illative and hears God saying that since they pay no regard to his authority when he reproves them by words, he will visit them for the contempt: he first tries whether men can be brought to repentance, and having tried all means by words comes to the exercise of his power. On the two times named, he rejects the reading that makes the first mean today, and joins day and night in a continued order, so that all are included from first to last; if any think those unpunished who are led later to vengeance they are mistaken, for as night follows day so some draw others after them into the same ruin. Keil and Delitzsch agree that the first word means by day rather than today, and add that the verb is used of the punishment and not the sin, and that the prophet named without an article refers to false prophets who practised prophesying as a trade and were very numerous in that kingdom. Ellicott divides the times by office, the priest discharging his function in the day and the prophet dreaming in the night, both tottering to their fall. Clarke reads the day as the most open and public manner, without snare or ambush, and takes the mother for the mother city, where Wesley makes her both the state and the assemblies of worship, and Ellicott simply the nation. Gill adds that the day may mean the day of prosperity, amidst great plenty, when such a fall was least expected.
6:
Who is destroyed comes first. Gill excludes those who are the people of God by special grace, since they cannot perish for want of knowledge, it being the determinate will of God to bring them to the truth; the verse speaks of the ten tribes, who were the people of God nationally and by profession. Keil and Delitzsch identify the speaker as Jehovah and the nation as his own, perishing for lack of the knowledge of God, which Israel might have drawn from the law in which God had revealed his counsel and will, but would not; it rejected the knowledge and forgot the law, and would be rejected and forgotten in consequence. Wesley reads the destruction as already begun, many having been cut off by an Assyrian king and many by a tyranny at home, and defines the missing knowledge as knowledge of God, of his law and providence, of his hatred of sin and power to punish it.

Whether priests or people are more to blame is the substance of the verse. Henry allows both readings. The people strove with the priests who should have taught them, and so were justly destroyed for lack of knowledge, since those who rebel against the light can expect to perish in the dark; or the charge lies on the priests, who should have been still teaching and did not, or did it so that it was as if they had not. Ignorance, he says, is so far from being the mother of devotion that it is the mother of destruction. He finds the aggravation in the relation, since God set his children to school to these teachers and they took no pains with them; and the root lies in the will, since the people did not learn and the priests did not teach not for want of light but because they hated it. Calvin divides the blame the same way and presses the second half harder. Though the idleness of the priests could not excuse the people, he inveighs against them for not performing their duty; but he asks how pure instruction failed to prevail, except that the people wished it should not. Their ignorance was gross, as with many ungodly men who not only love darkness but draw it around them that they may have some excuse. God had kindled among them the light of celestial wisdom in the law, as though he shone forth from heaven, and they perished through ignorance only because they closed their eyes against it. The people perished without knowledge, Calvin says, because they would perish. As for the priests, he calls it extreme wickedness, as though they wished to subvert the sacred order of God, that they sought the honour of the office without the office itself. Clarke states the loss plainly, that they have knowledge neither of God nor of sacred things nor of their own danger, and walk on blindly and perish, though they might have become wise had they not rejected the means of improvement.

Who is addressed in the singular is the last point. Clarke supposes that if the reading is sound there must be a reference to some particular priest well known, unless the whole priesthood is meant under the name. Wesley takes it as a change of audience, the prophet passing from people to priests and speaking to them as one person, and makes the children the whole kingdom of the ten tribes. Ellicott addresses the priest directly, as the man who should have kept the knowledge alive in their hearts, and has the controversy repudiate a whole priesthood which had inclined to calf-worship, vacillated over Baal and connived at moral offences. But he offers a second reading, which he says most commentators prefer, in which the people are addressed, and the threat is the cessation of that priesthood every member of the theocracy ought to have maintained.
7:
What increased is read broadly. Gill allows two senses, that as the children of the priests increased and grew up they sinned, imitating their parents, so that they were as many sinners as they were persons and not one to be excepted, or that the increase was in riches, honour, dignity and authority, and that they sinned the more for it, which shows their ingratitude. Keil and Delitzsch take the phrase of the nation growing into a powerful people with increasing wealth, and explain why prosperity made things worse: the nation attributed to its own idols the blessings on which its prosperity rested and looked on them as the fruit and reward of its worship, so that growing prosperity only strengthened the delusion and estranged it further from the living God. Calvin says the same of the whole people rather than of the priests alone, since the prophet had already separated the crimes of the priests and is here returning to a general proposition; they had increased in number and in wealth, were prosperous under a certain reign and thought themselves extremely happy because filled with every abundance, and grew wanton on it like a well-fed horse that kicks against his own master, a comparison used long before in a song. Wesley includes kings, priests and people together, and puts it that sin grew with their wealth and honour, and that they turned all in which they might have gloried above others into sin.

On the exchange of glory for shame, Keil and Delitzsch say simply that the greatness or wealth of Ephraim is what will be turned. Clarke makes the exchange answer an earlier one, since the idolaters at Dan and Bethel had already changed the glory of God into the similitude of an ox that eats grass, and adds that in the day of wrath their calf-gods shall not deliver them.

What the priests eat is the sharper question. Keil and Delitzsch note that the reproof now advances from the sin of the whole nation to the sin of the priesthood, and take the sin of the people for the sin-offering, whose flesh the priests were commanded to eat in order to wipe away the sin of the people; the keeping of that command became itself a sin from the fact that they directed their longing towards the transgression of the people, wishing their sins to increase so that they might receive a good supply of sacrificial meat. Clarke reads the same word as the sin-offering and adds that it was eaten though offered contrary to the law, their hearts being set on iniquity. Wesley agrees that the sin is probably the sin-offering, in which the priest had his share, and calls them covetous, luxurious, idolatrous priests who minister to the idols. Gill offers the reading with alternatives: their fault was either that they ate what belonged to the true priests, or that they ate with no concern to instruct the people, regarding only good eating and drinking and a voluptuous life, or that the feasts meant were those made in the temples of the idols, of which the priests greatly partook, so that they were partakers not of the banquets only but of the sins.

Calvin refuses the whole line. To render the word sin-offerings, he says, is to destroy the force of the passage, which is that the priests gained their living through the superstition of the people; and the iniquity named next means idolatry, to which the priests raised up the heart of the people and by which they attached them. He notes that the pronouns of the verse may be referred either to the priests or to the people, and that the words will bear both, though in a different sense.
9:
The levelling of priest and people is taken as a sentence on both. Gill finds no difference between them, the one as greedy of intemperance and uncleanness as the other, whether at their festivals or in common life, though the priests ought to have given good instruction and set good example; being equally guilty, they will be alike in punishment. Clarke puts the same in a couplet, that the priest is a wanderer from the narrow way and it is no wonder the silly sheep should stray, and says that both will be punished, as both are equally bad. Keil and Delitzsch add the reason: since the priests had abused their office for the purpose of filling their own bellies, they would perish along with the nation, and though the suffixes in the last clauses refer to the priest, the retribution threatened falls on the people also. Calvin states the double guilt sharply. God will spare neither, for the priest abused the honour conferred on him, appointed over the Church to preserve the people in piety and holy life and breaking through every right principle; and the people for their part wished to have such teachers, that is, mute ones. He knows a further reading, that God would rob the priests of their honour so that they should differ nothing from the people, and allows it to be true, but denies the inference some draw from it, that no one but the priests is threatened here; the subject, he says, expands wider than that.

Why eating should not satisfy is answered from the appetite and from the blessing. Calvin traces it to the vice already named, since the priests gaped for gain and their only care was to satisfy their appetites, and their cupidity was insatiable, which was also why they conceded a sinful liberty to the people. Then he generalises: men are not sustained by plenty or abundance of provisions but rather by the blessing of God, and a person may devour much and the quantity, however large, may not satisfy him, the staff of bread being broken so that much eating does not feed. The priests thought it a happy time when they gathered great booty from every quarter, and God declares that it would prove empty and useless to them. Gill keeps the priests as the subject and offers three readings: that what they ate of the sacrifices and of the idol feasts did not nourish them, or that their appetites remained greedy for more, or that a famine is meant, at the siege of the capital or in the captivity, when men who had lived voluptuously would have too little to satisfy them. Clarke says only that whatever means they use to gratify themselves shall be ineffectual. Keil and Delitzsch divide the verse between the two parties, the first clause still referring to the priests and drawn from an older threat, while the word that follows refers to the whole nation and must be taken in its literal sense, as the antithesis requires; and the final clause, that they have given up giving heed to God, applies to priests and people alike.

On the barrenness Wesley states the alternatives plainly, that they shall not increase the number of their children, either the women not bearing or the children not living. Calvin makes it the frustration of a design: however much they give the reins to promiscuous lusts, God will not suffer them to propagate, so far shall they be from increasing by lawful marriage that were they everywhere to indulge in illicit intercourse they would still continue barren. The lesson he draws is that the ungodly are deceived when they think they can obtain their wishes by wicked and unlawful means, since the Lord will frustrate them.
11:
What the heart means here, and what takes it away, is settled quickly. Clarke says the two debaucheries generally go together and that they darken the understanding, deprave the judgment and pervert the will; Wesley that they deprive men of understanding; Ellicott that the heart is the whole inner life, consumed by these indulgences. Gill offers three senses of the taking away: that intemperance besots men and makes them downright fools, or takes the heart away from following the Lord, or occupies the heart and fills it so that it prefers sensual pleasures to the fear and love of God; he thinks the words chiefly respect the priests. Keil and Delitzsch make the sentence the hinge of the passage, a maxim introducing the description of idolatrous conduct that follows, and observe that what is true of licentiousness, that it weakens the mental power, shows itself in the folly of the idolatry into which the nation has fallen. Calvin denies that it is a general truth at all. Most regard it as a proverbial saying, that wantonness and wine deprive men of their right mind; he restricts it to these people and supplies a cause from their history: the kingdom was then very opulent and full of luxury, and the question how they came to be so senseless is answered by their excesses, so that God means they abused his blessings and were blinded by them.

That they are still called the people of God is not lost on two voices. Calvin says the title is used not to honour them but to increase their sin, since the perfidy is the more heinous in those who, having been chosen, forsook their heavenly Father; the sting of it is that this people, who ought to be his, consult their own wood. He turns it on his readers, that our guilt will be the more grievous if we do not continue in the pure worship of God, having been designed to be his peculiar flock. Keil and Delitzsch note the same antithesis more briefly, that the reproof is strengthened by the words my nation, the nation of the living God.

What was consulted is described with some care. Gill takes the stocks for wooden gods, mere blocks without life or sense, and reports two possibilities: that the reference is to the material of which an idol was made, the trunk of a tree, as a poet makes an idol say that it was once a fig-tree trunk and useless wood, or to sticks of wood with no form given them at all, since ancient idolaters are said to have venerated pieces of wood, one people worshipping for their goddess a piece never hewn or planed. Clarke says they consulted their wooden gods and used divination by rods. Ellicott reports the same explanation from an ancient writer, that rods were set upright and, after incantations, allowed to fall, the forecast being read from the manner of their falling; but he suggests the staff may rather refer, like the stocks, to the idol itself, since a Canaanite goddess was worshipped under that form. Calvin hears an allusion to blindness in the second clause, since as a blind man asks his staff, so these people asked counsel of theirs; he allows that particular superstitions may be pointed at, augurs having used a staff and diviners in the East probably employing one in their incantations. Henry supplies the disposition behind the practice: they have a spirit of whoredoms, a strong inclination to that sin, the bent and bias of their hearts that way, and this causes them to err; the errors of the judgment, he says, are commonly owing to the corrupt affections, since men have a good opinion of sin because they have a disposition towards it. They consulted their idols as oracles, using the arts of divination learned from their idolatrous priests.
13:
The trees and hilltops are what the earlier charge of fornication meant. Calvin makes the point explicitly: the prophet is defining what he had condemned under that word, that they worshipped God under trees and on high places, and the definition was necessary, because men will not easily give way when they can adduce some colour for their sins. The superstitious cry out when their modes of worship are condemned and ask whether it can be fornication when they are worshipping God, since whatever is done from inconsiderate zeal they think free from blame; so the prophet had to show openly that though they supposed themselves to be worshipping with pious zeal, they were committing fornication all the same. Gill notes that the altars stood on the highest part of the mountains, nearest the heavens, and Ellicott that hilltops were continually chosen for such temples. Ellicott corrects two of the trees, the poplar being the white poplar and not the shrub named by the Greek version, and the third the terebinth; Clarke traces the name of the oak to a root meaning to be strong, and notes its Latin name means strength. On the good shadow he supplies three reasons for what follows: the deities were worshipped by prostitution, much was drunk in the worship so that the passions were inflamed, and the thick groves were favourable to it.

Why the women are passed over is answered variously. Gill offers two, that they are not punished at all, so that they go on further, or that they are not punished yet, because it was by example that they were led into it; and he reports that some render the clause as a question, whether God shall not punish the daughters, to which the answer is that he will, and not them only but their parents and husbands, who deserve severer correction. Ellicott says plainly that the women are more sinned against than sinning. Keil and Delitzsch say the elder ones did still worse, and quote an older writer that the fornications were so many that all punishment ceased, in despair of amendment; they add that at the next words God turns away from the reckless nation as unworthy of further address, and proceeds to speak of it in the third person. Clarke reads the silence as the worst sign of all: why be stricken any more when they will only revolt more; and when God in judgment removes his judgments, the case of a people is desperate, since while there is hope there is correction. Calvin makes the withholding itself the punishment: the man who does not worship God shall have an adulterous wife at home and daughters boldly playing the wanton, and God will not correct them, wishing them exposed to infamy; for the rule stands that he who honours God will be honoured and he who despises his name made contemptible.

The separation in the next clause divides them. Calvin knows a reading that takes the verb of husbands dividing from their wives, and rejects it: the prophet means they separated themselves from God, as a wife does who leaves her husband, so that the word is used allegorically, or at least metaphorically. The reason, he says, is not understood by those who take the passage literally of adulteries, and their mistake is proved by the clause that follows, since the separation he means is that they sacrificed with strumpets, which they could not do without violating the faith they had pledged to God. Ellicott and Clarke keep it literal, Ellicott referring the words to the sensuality of the rites and the women who dedicated themselves to those impurities, Clarke to debaucheries he will not describe. Wesley states the moral in a line: the husbands and fathers are the examples to their wives and daughters, and the ignorant people who do not know God shall be utterly ruined.
15:
The verse turns from accusation to warning, and the question is whom it warns. Keil and Delitzsch describe the turn: if Israel will not desist from idolatry, Judah ought to beware of sharing the guilt by making pilgrimages to the places of idolatrous worship in that kingdom. Clarke states the contrast plainly, that Israel was totally dissolute and Judah was not, and that she is exhorted to maintain her integrity: if the one will go to what was once the house of God and is now the house of iniquity, let not the other imitate her. Ellicott hears in it a warning to Judah of the peril of her neighbour, and perhaps a hint at the apostasy of some of her own kings. Gill gives the same sense and offers a second: the whole may be directed to Israel, as an exhortation that though they had given into such abominations they should be careful not to make Judah stumble into the same sins, which would aggravate their own guilt by drawing others in.

Calvin takes the warning as the point of the verse and draws two lessons from it. He complains that Judah also was infected, though the Lord had wonderfully kept her from pollutions of this kind, and sets out the comparison: it is no wonder that Israel plays the wanton, having long shaken off the yoke, but it is not to be endured that Judah should fall away into the same abominations. From this he concludes first how difficult it is to continue untouched when men come into contact with pollutions, since vicinity brings contagion; the two kingdoms were separated, and the one was still corrupted by the diseases of the other. There is nothing, he says, we are so disposed to do as to forsake true religion, since there is naturally in us a perverse lust for mixing false forms of worship with it, and every one is here a teacher to himself; what then is likely to happen when Satan stimulates us? Let all who are neighbours to idolaters beware. His second conclusion is that the guilt of those rightly taught is not to be extenuated when they associate with the blind, since God had carried the torch of light before this people and had not suffered sound doctrine to be extinguished among them.

The two places named are given their histories. Clarke recalls that the first was where the covenant of circumcision was renewed when the people passed over Jordan, and was afterwards rendered infamous by the worship of idols. Wesley says it was chosen by a king, or by the idolaters who came after him, for the solemn worship of their idols, and that the second was the place where Jacob lodged and which he named the house of God, but that when it was made the seat of calf-worship it became the house of vanity. Keil and Delitzsch identify the first more narrowly, not the Gilgal in the valley of the Jordan but the northern one upon the mountains, whose name survives in a village. Ellicott counts three places of that name in one book and a fourth elsewhere, and settles on the one that had long been the headquarters of Joshua and acquired importance in the days of Samuel as a place of sacrificial worship and of the dispensation of justice. Of the second he notes that it had a grand history before two prophets began calling it by the altered name meaning house of vanity; and he reports a variant, that one Greek manuscript reads instead the name of the city that was the seat of sun-worship, from which the calf-worship may have been derived, while another agrees with the received tradition. Wesley alone explains the last clause, taking the oath for the whole worship of God, which the prophet warns them not to blend with their idolatries.
16:
The heifer is an animal that will not take the yoke. Gill draws three pictures from it: a refractory beast which breaks through every fence, as they broke the laws of God; one unaccustomed to the yoke, which wriggles its neck from under it; and one which, though yoked, slides back in the furrows. The figure is chosen the rather, he adds, because the objects of their worship were calves, so that they are upbraided with their idols. Clarke has the same untractable beast that pulls back rather than draw, and Wesley one that, grown lusty and wanton, will neither endure the yoke nor be confined in her allowed pastures. Ellicott would render the word more correctly as stubborn. Calvin canvasses the alternatives: some render it a straying heifer, and it may be rendered wanton, while others intend a defection, because the people had receded from God; but he prefers the sense of one petulant or lascivious, since the punishment which follows agrees with that.

Whether the punishment is mercy or judgment divides them, and most take it hard. Keil and Delitzsch make it the granting of a wish: since Israel would not submit to the yoke of the divine law, it should have what it desired, and God would feed it like a lamb which in a wide field becomes the prey of wild beasts, giving it up to the freedom of banishment among the nations. Clarke calls the words a species of irony, since they may sport themselves in the empire into which they will be carried captive; Wesley makes the large place a wilderness with no rest, safety or provision. Ellicott reports that one commentator takes the clause as tender commiseration, but says most understand it unfavourably, of a leading forth into the desolate wilderness as a prey to wild beasts, or into the loneliness a lamb would feel in a boundless pasture. Calvin allows both senses. On the first the Lord would leave them in their luxuries to gorge themselves according to their lust, a dreadful punishment, since it is a fearful thing when God suffers men to wanton without limit; on the second, which he prefers, God would so scatter them that they might be as a lamb in a spacious place, since it is peculiar to sheep to continue under a shepherd, and one driven into solitude shows by its bleating that it is seeking its flock, being no solitary animal.

Who is to leave Ephraim alone is the last question. Keil and Delitzsch take the phrase from ordinary speech, meaning that it may do as it likes or remain as it is, every attempt to bring the nation from its idolatry being vain; they deny the words need be addressed to the prophets at all, the sense being that it may continue in its idolatry, since punishment will not long be delayed. Clarke calls them irreclaimable, to be left to the consequences of their own conduct. Ellicott has the prophet calling on Judah to leave Ephraim to himself, and reports that two Jewish interpreters make it the appeal of God to the prophet, to leave Israel to her fate so that her eyes might perhaps be opened to her doom. Calvin takes that reading and makes it a dismissal: God, as if wearied, bids his prophet rest, since he prevails nothing with this people. He had set him over them to lead them to repentance if they could be reformed, and now, seeing the labour in vain, tells him there is no use wearying himself, for they are wholly incurable. In saying they are joined to idols, he adds, the prophet means an alliance that cannot be broken, alluding to the marriage he spoke of before: they had been joined to God, and there was hope of recovery until they clave so fast to their idols that they could not be drawn away.
18:
The first clause is obscure and each handles it differently. Gill offers three renderings: that the drink is sour in their stomachs, they having drunk more than they can digest, which makes the clause a charge of drunkenness; or that their drink is gone, having turned to vinegar, which would express the general corruption of their manners and religion; or that their drink is refractory, that is, made them so and caused them to depart from the worship of God. Keil and Delitzsch take the verb to mean degenerating, and the noun for intoxicating wine, here standing for its effect. They report the alternative that takes the verb in its usual sense of departing and reads the sentence conditionally, that when their intoxication is gone they commit whoredom, and reject it: it is intoxication which leads to licentiousness and not temperance, and the emphatic strengthening of the next verb does not suit such a reading. Clarke would rather render it that he is gone after their wine, the enticements of idolatry having carried them away; Wesley simply that their wine is corrupt and hurtful.

Calvin treats the clause as metaphor. Their drink has become putrid, he says, meaning that they had so intemperately given themselves to every kind of wickedness that all things among them had become fetid; and he presses the comparison, since the drunken emit a disgusting smell and are never satisfied until they spew up what they have taken. The prophet does not speak of wine at all, he is certain, but means by drunkenness the unbridled licentiousness then prevailing: allowing themselves everything without shame, they seemed like drunken men. He follows the same metaphor into the next clause, that by wantoning they have become wanton, reproaching them on two accounts, that they cast aside every shame like the drunken and that they had abandoned themselves to idols.

On the rulers Clarke works the words closely. He would read that they have loved shame rather than that they love with shame, so that they glory in their abominations, and thinks it better still to read that they have loved gifts; and he notices that the word for rulers is literally shields, so that those who should have been the defence of the people were those by whom justice was perverted. Wesley finds shameful oppression and bribery among them, the whoredom continual from one reign down to the prophet.

The last verse turns on who binds whom. Gill gives the received sense first, that the wind has bound up Israel in its wings, the wrath of God, or the enemy, coming like a whirlwind to carry them out of their own land, the past tense standing for the future because of the certainty of it. Then he reports four commentators who render it the other way, that she has bound up the wind in her wings, meaning they had laboured in vain in their idolatrous worship, as if a man should gather the wind into the skirts of his garment and find nothing when he opens them. Calvin prefers the second as better suited to the subject: men could never despise the word of God so audaciously were they not supporting their minds with vain confidence, and being unmindful of their condition they attempt to fly as if by the wind, so that when they proudly raise themselves they have no support but wind. On the first reading he allows either tense, a storm that will sweep the people away or one that already has. Clarke has a parching wind blasting them in their borders, or a captivity as rapid as a blight, and admits the last two verses are very obscure. Wesley has the whirlwind of the wrath of God seizing the old adulteress and carrying some of her children away already, and closes on the last clause: what they made their confidence shall be their shame.
